standard.title: Interpret and translate for intercultural understanding
standard.description: apply strategies to interpret and translate non-verbal, spoken and written interactions and texts to convey meaning and intercultural understanding in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have developed and begun to apply interpretation and translation strategies in familiar contexts — including dictionary use, cognate recognition, contextual inferencing and understanding word-for-word limits (AC9LS8EC05). They have not yet applied these strategies in unfamiliar contexts or with the explicit goal of conveying intercultural understanding.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students apply a range of interpretation and translation strategies to non-verbal, spoken and written texts in familiar and unfamiliar contexts, conveying meaning and intercultural understanding — including recognising culturally embedded concepts, evaluating translation tools, and managing communication challenges.

nodes.label: Translating culturally embedded meaning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and interpret expressions or concepts in the target language that are culturally embedded — where meaning cannot be conveyed through word-for-word translation.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and explain at least one target language expression or concept that requires cultural knowledge to translate accurately.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and interpret culturally embedded expressions, idioms and concepts; explain what is 'lost in translation' and why; distinguish between cases where a target language concept has an English equivalent and where it encodes a culturally specific idea.
wider: Research a concept embedded in the target language that has no direct English equivalent — explain the cultural or social context that gives it meaning
Compare how cultural concepts are translated or left untranslated in published bilingual texts — identify the translator's choices and evaluate their effectiveness
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that some target language meaning is culturally embedded — and cannot be accessed through linguistic analysis alone — is the conceptual shift that distinguishes interpretation from translation. Students who have not made this shift will approach all translation as word substitution, producing inaccurate and culturally insensitive renderings that cannot satisfy EC05's intercultural understanding demand.

response_modes.reason: The culturally embedded concept insight requires explicit teaching — students do not arrive at it through exposure alone. Case studies of specific culturally embedded expressions, with discussion of the cultural context required to understand them, build the conceptual move.

Exposure to culturally embedded concepts across diverse target language communities (regional, national, diasporic) prevents students from assuming one cultural frame for the whole target language community.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Culturally embedded meaning is where language learning becomes intercultural understanding in the fullest sense. Students who can identify and explain these concepts have qualitatively different linguistic and cultural competence — they understand that languages are not codes for the same underlying meaning but systems that construct meaning differently.
success_criteria: Can identify at least one target language expression that requires cultural knowledge to translate and explain what that knowledge is
Can distinguish between a translation challenge caused by linguistic difference and one caused by cultural difference

nodes.label: Evaluating translation tools and strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of translation tools and strategies, including digital translation tools, for different contexts and purposes.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate one digital translation of a short target language text — identify at least two errors or limitations and explain what the tool missed.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate translation strategies and tools across different text types and purposes; conduct 'back translations' to test accuracy; identify where automated tools produce awkward, inaccurate or culturally inappropriate renderings; develop personal evaluation criteria for translation quality.
wider: Compare multiple translation tools or strategies (dictionary, automated, peer, self) for the same text — analyse differences and develop a framework for choosing an appropriate tool
Translate a short text for a real purpose (e.g. a bilingual resource for the school community) and document translation decisions and challenges

response_modes.reason: Evaluating translation quality requires criteria — students need to develop explicit evaluative frameworks (accuracy, cultural appropriateness, register, audience fit) before assessment is meaningful. Guided evaluation tasks with discussion of the criteria build this analytical capacity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Critical evaluation of digital translation tools is a genuinely contemporary and transferable skill. Students who develop principled translation evaluation criteria are better equipped to use these tools responsibly across all language encounters beyond the classroom.
success_criteria: Can identify at least two specific errors or limitations in a digital translation of a target language text
Can explain what type of knowledge (linguistic, cultural, contextual) the tool lacked to produce an accurate translation

nodes.label: Managing communication challenges
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply repair and adaptation strategies to manage communication challenges in the target language — including in unfamiliar contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate at least one communication repair strategy in a target language interaction (e.g. rephrasing, asking for repetition, using a non-verbal cue to signal misunderstanding).
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of strategies to manage communication breakdowns — rephrasing, asking for clarification, adjusting formality, switching between modes; identify formality levels in spoken and written texts and adjust appropriately; manage unfamiliar communication contexts with limited language resources.
wider: Reflect on a real or simulated communication challenge in the target language — identify what broke down and evaluate which repair strategy was most effective
Investigate how register and formality conventions in the target language signal social relationships — practise adjusting formality across different simulated contexts

response_modes.reason: Communication repair draws on the full range of interpretation and translation strategies from nodes 1–2 plus the conversational maintenance skills from EC01–EC02. It represents the applied endpoint of the mediating strand — using strategies to keep meaning-making alive when language resources are incomplete.

success_criteria: Demonstrates at least one successful repair or adaptation strategy in a target language interaction
Can identify formality levels in at least two target language texts and explain what language features signal each
